clue.text: Picks up superfluous ink well

definitions.text: Picks up superfluous ink well

parts.words: Picks up superfluous ink well
parts.note: read as praise for a good mopper of excess ink: the absorbent sheet pressed over wet writing does exactly that

explanation.surface: Someone is complimented on how tidily they deal with spilt ink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ink well' looks like the inkpot; read 'well' as the adverb, saying the thing soaks up excess ink efficiently.
explanation.definitionFit: Absorbent sheets laid over fresh handwriting soak up surplus wet ink, which is their whole purpose.

clue.text: He wants to get something from the house detective. Tries to find him

definitions.text: He wants to get something from the house detective. Tries to find him

parts.words: He wants to get something from the house detective. Tries to find him
parts.note: the housebreaker wants to take something from a house, and the detective tries to track him down

explanation.surface: A man hopes to extract information from the house detective, who is looking for him.
explanation.walkthrough: The run-on 'house detective' is a false phrase: the full stop belongs after 'house', and 'detective tries to find him' is a separate thought.
explanation.definitionFit: A housebreaker enters homes to steal property, and police detectives pursue such thieves.

clue.text: Can get at the contents with them

definitions.text: Can get at the contents with them

parts.words: Can get at the contents with them
parts.note: 'Can' reads as the verb 'is able to' but is really the tin; tools for tins reach what is inside

explanation.surface: With these tools a person is able to reach what is inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' is the noun, a tin: tin-openers let you get at its contents.
explanation.definitionFit: Tin-openers and bottle-openers are devices for getting into sealed containers.

clue.text: They're driven to join up

definitions.text: They're driven to join up

parts.words: They're driven to join up
parts.note: sounds like conscripts forced to enlist, but hammered metal spikes are driven in to fasten pieces together

explanation.surface: Reluctant recruits are forced into enlisting.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal pins hammered into wood are used to fix pieces of timber together.

clue.text: Birds' heads from peacocks, larks, owls, vultures, eagles, ravens & starlings

definitions.text: Birds'

indicators.note: the heads of these listed birds are their first letters, taken one from each word in turn

parts.words: peacocks, larks, owls, vultures, eagles, ravens & starlings

explanation.surface: Somebody collects the heads of a whole aviary of different birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Birds'' is the definition (the plural, with the possessive read as part of the surface); the ampersand is just a link before the last bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Plovers are wading shorebirds such as the lapwing and golden plover.

clue.text: In the old army, putting on a charge like this usually resulted in getting shot!

definitions.text: In the old army, putting on a charge like this usually resulted in getting shot!

parts.words: In the old army, putting on a charge like this usually resulted in getting shot!
parts.note: being put on a charge is military discipline, but in old muskets a charge of powder was put in the pan before firing

explanation.surface: A soldier in the old days who was put on a charge could expect to be executed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting on a charge' means a disciplinary offence; in flintlock days it meant adding powder to the pan so the gun would fire a shot.
explanation.definitionFit: Old firearms needed a small dose of powder in the pan to ignite the main load when fired.

clue.text: All of a flutter, Her Majesty coming to stay

definitions.text: All of a flutter, Her Majesty coming to stay

parts.words: All of a flutter, Her Majesty coming to stay
parts.note: sounds like a host excited by a royal visit, but the monarch's flag is hoisted and flutters wherever she is in residence

explanation.surface: A nervous host is in a tizzy because the Queen is visiting.
explanation.walkthrough: The British monarch's personal flag is flown over any building where the sovereign is staying.
explanation.definitionFit: This banner is the sovereign's own flag, flown above a residence while the monarch is present.

clue.text: The code set forth in the Book of Samuel?

definitions.text: The code set forth in the Book of Samuel?

parts.words: The code set forth in the Book of Samuel?
parts.note: a Bible book suggests scripture, but this Samuel is the American inventor whose telegraph signalling system bears his surname

explanation.surface: A question about a law code laid down in an Old Testament book.
explanation.walkthrough: The Book of Samuel is a red herring: Samuel Morse devised the dot-and-dash telegraph code.
explanation.definitionFit: The dot-and-dash telegraphy system is named after its inventor, Samuel Morse.

clue.text: Looks pretty, displayed in a case of shellfish

definitions.text: Looks pretty, displayed in a case of shellfish

parts.words: Looks pretty, displayed in a case of shellfish
parts.note: suggests seafood in a display case, but the iridescent lining of an oyster shell is the pretty material on show

explanation.surface: Shellfish look attractive arranged in a display cabinet.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'case' is the shell itself, whose lining is the lustrous nacre.
explanation.definitionFit: Nacre, the shimmering inner layer of mollusc shells, is prized as a decorative material.

clue.text: Feeling hostile

definitions.text: Feeling hostile

parts.words: Feeling hostile
parts.note: read as a noun phrase, a hostile feeling, rather than the adjective it seems

explanation.walkthrough: 'Feeling' is the noun here: a hostile feeling, i.e. enmity.
explanation.definitionFit: Enmity or strong dislike is a feeling of hostility towards someone.

clue.text: They're done for — litigants who think they've been wronged

definitions.text: They're done for — litigants who think they've been wronged

parts.words: They're done for — litigants who think they've been wronged
parts.note: 'done for' suggests ruined, but deeds are things done, and lawsuits are what aggrieved litigants bring

explanation.surface: Litigants who feel wronged are finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Done for' is not 'finished': deeds are things done, and lawsuits are things done for litigants.
explanation.definitionFit: Deeds are things done, and in law suits brought by claimants are also called by this name.

clue.text: Yet such stories have the lowest truth content

definitions.text: Yet such stories have the lowest truth content

parts.words: Yet such stories have the lowest truth content
parts.note: the paradox: tall stories are exaggerations, so the most extreme ones, highest in stature, are least truthful

explanation.surface: A remark that some stories contain the least truth of all.
explanation.walkthrough: A tall story is an exaggeration; the superlative is paradoxically the least true.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall tale is an exaggerated, unlikely story; the superlative is the most far-fetched of them.

clue.text: Ie.,claps turn that's out of the ordinary

definitions.text: out of the ordinary

indicators.note: a turn here is a twist or change of order, so the letters of the preceding words are rearranged

parts.words: Ie.,claps

explanation.surface: A performer's act, with its applause, is something unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' rearranges IECLAPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something special is exceptional, unlike the usual run of things.

clue.text: Peers brought before London court

definitions.text: Peers brought before London court

parts.words: Peers brought before London court
parts.note: sounds like nobles on trial, but put the noblemen before the word court and you get a London district

explanation.surface: Members of the nobility are put on trial in a London court.
explanation.walkthrough: Earls Court is a district of west London; the peers literally come before 'court' in the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Noblemen ranking above viscounts are members of the peerage, hence peers.

clue.text: It can be heaved in public -that's an error!

definitions.text: It can be heaved in public -that's an error!

parts.words: It can be heaved in public -that's an error!
parts.note: a sigh is heaved; heaved over a public sight, the whole thing is a mistake through failing to notice

explanation.surface: Someone sighs heavily in public and calls it a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: A sigh is heaved; split as OVER SIGH-T, but the whole is a slip made by not noticing.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip made through failing to notice something is an error of omission.

clue.text: Eastern vessel seen going about for a Jewish

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Eastern vessel seen going about for a Jewish (7)': the definition is cut short (presumably 'Jewish sect'), and no scan or search gives the missing word; wordplay E + SS + reversed SEEN.
annotationWithheld.clue: Eastern vessel seen going about for a Jewish

clue.text: One who behaves tyrannically gets us down

definitions.text: One who behaves tyrannically gets us down

parts.words: One who behaves tyrannically gets us down
parts.note: a tyrant crushes and depresses people, which is exactly what keeping people down by force means

explanation.surface: A tyrant grinds us all down.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep people subjugated and harshly ruled is to weigh them down with tyranny.

clue.text: Grounds for conducting tests

definitions.text: Grounds for conducting tests

parts.words: Grounds for conducting tests
parts.note: 'grounds' suggests reasons or justification, but here it is literal testing sites, as in weapons ranges

explanation.surface: Reasons for running some examinations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grounds' looks like reasons, but proving grounds are areas used for testing vehicles or weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Proving grounds are sites set aside for trials of weapons or vehicles.

clue.text: Turned out all right? Better than that!

definitions.text: Turned out all right? Better than that!

parts.words: Turned out all right? Better than that!
parts.note: 'turned out' means dressed; better than merely well dressed is stylish and graceful

explanation.surface: Asked whether things worked out fine, someone says they went even better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned out' is about dress, not outcome: more than just well turned out.
explanation.definitionFit: Stylish, graceful and refined in appearance is more than merely neatly dressed.

clue.text: Stick said to encourage cricketers, by the look of it

definitions.text: Stick said to encourage cricketers, by the look of it

parts.words: Stick said to encourage cricketers, by the look of it
parts.note: split visually into two words it looks like a cry urging batsmen to keep batting, while as one word it is a stick

explanation.surface: Words of encouragement are shouted to a cricket team.
explanation.walkthrough: Seen as 'bat on', it reads like a call to batsmen to keep going; 'by the look of it' means by its written form.
explanation.definitionFit: A conductor's or relay runner's short rod is a type of stick.

clue.text: Plainly impudent to do something in such a way!

definitions.text: Plainly impudent to do something in such a way!

parts.words: Plainly impudent to do something in such a way!
parts.note: describes doing something openly and shamelessly, with no attempt at concealment

explanation.surface: Someone is told off for doing a thing so cheekily.
explanation.definitionFit: Flagrant, unashamedly obvious behaviour is open and brazen, plainly cheeky.

clue.text: Flat rimmed article used to serve refreshment

definitions.text: Flat rimmed article used to serve refreshment

parts.words: Flat rimmed article used to serve refreshment
parts.note: a flat board with a raised edge on which cups of a hot drink are carried

explanation.surface: A description of an item for bringing drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat board with a raised lip is what cups and pots of a hot drink are carried on.

clue.text: One registered by an opponent

definitions.text: One registered by an opponent

parts.words: One registered by an opponent
parts.note: sounds like a voter or member signed up, but an objection is formally lodged by someone who disagrees

explanation.surface: Someone is enrolled by a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Registered' looks like enrolled; one registers an objection.
explanation.definitionFit: An objector formally lodges an objection, the formal expression of dissent.

clue.text: Point to a rose bush

definitions.text: Point to a rose bush

parts.words: Point to a rose bush
parts.note: 'point to' sounds like indicating, but a sharp point found on a rose stem is meant

explanation.surface: An instruction to indicate a rose bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point to' looks like a verb; read it as a noun phrase, a sharp point belonging to a rose.
explanation.definitionFit: A prickle on a rose stem is a sharp spike, a natural point.

clue.text: Falls for honeymooner in the States

definitions.text: Falls for honeymooner in the States

parts.words: Falls for honeymooner in the States
parts.note: 'falls for' suggests falling in love, but famous waterfalls are a classic American honeymoon destination

explanation.surface: Someone in America falls in love with a newlywed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falls for' looks like falling in love; it is the waterfall on the US–Canada border, long a honeymoon spot.
explanation.definitionFit: The great waterfall on the US–Canada border is a traditional destination for newlyweds.

clue.text: A backwards rotating, pointless Pole may upset the workers

definitions.text: A backwards rotating, pointless Pole may upset the workers

parts.words: A

indicators.note: the compass point north is dropped, so the word loses one point of the compass
the preceding word is to be read from its end to its start

parts.words: rotating
Pole
parts.note: S is the south pole

explanation.surface: A Pole spinning the wrong way is aimlessly stirring up the labour force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backwards' turns ROTATING into GNITATOR; 'pointless' removes N (north, a compass point) to give GITATOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Political activists stir up unrest among workforces, which is what troublemakers in industry do.

clue.text: Is right about corrosive chemical having pungent smell

definitions.text: having pungent smell

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is placed round the other

parts.words: corrosive chemical
parts.note: an acid is a corrosive chemical

parts.words: right

explanation.surface: A corrosive substance gives off a sharp odour.
explanation.definitionFit: A sharp, bitter, stinging odour or taste is described as pungent.

clue.text: Presumably, capital for such businesses can be easily raised!

definitions.text: Presumably, capital for such businesses can be easily raised!

parts.words: Presumably, capital for such businesses can be easily raised!
parts.note: 'raised' suggests fundraising, but lifting something weightless is easy, so firms making small goods are joked about

explanation.surface: An investor says funding for certain firms is easy to come by.
explanation.walkthrough: Raising capital means getting funding; the joke takes 'light' as not heavy, so it is easy to lift.
explanation.definitionFit: Manufacturing of small consumer goods rather than heavy machinery is called by this name.
